prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening the regime of 10^-18 fractional uncertainty in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks satisfy the 'discovery or invention' criterion cleanly and, in my view, more cleanly than any other shortlisted entry. The invention is concrete: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light shift so that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel. Ye's group then carried the concept to the 10^-18 level and showed that many-body effects can be controlled rather than merely tolerated. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), the interpretation is stable, and consequences are already visible in tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the discussion of redefining the second. Six of the eight opening ballots place it in the top three and two place it first, and the support comes from atomic physics, particle physics, condensed matter and experimental colleagues alike rather than from a single camp. A two-person prize also avoids the crowded-credit problems that affect several other entries. I should be open that my own opening first choice was B019 (aberration-corrected electron optics). No other colleague ranked it first, and given my field I discount my own enthusiasm for it; I do not think I can argue that it should displace B035 on this record.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is scope and precedent. The 2005 prize recognised the optical frequency comb and precision spectroscopy (Hall and Hansch), and the lattice clock rests on the comb as its counting mechanism, so some will see this as a continuation of an already honoured line. Ion-clock groups (for example Wineland's, honoured in 2012 for other work) and the Lemonde, Lisdat and Takamoto groups also made real contributions to performance and to Sr and Yb clocks, so the claim that Katori and Ye are the only credit-worthy names is a simplification. Finally, the case for a redefinition of the second is not yet settled, and a committee might prefer to wait to see which clock species and scheme the metrology community adopts.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect first because it opened a conceptually new class of matter with reach across materials, photonics, cold atoms and devices, and sees the HgTe experiment as making it concrete.
responses.response: I take the conceptual reach seriously, and as a materials person I have watched topological surface and edge states change how people search for new compounds. But I weigh two things against it. First, the 2016 prize for topological phases of matter already recognised the underlying framework, so the novelty question is sharper here than for lattice clocks. Second, the attribution problem is real and Mehlig names it himself: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is the specific bridge between Kane-Mele theory and Molenkamp's experiment, and the three credited names cannot express it. I therefore keep B008 as my first alternative but not my preferred choice. If colleagues convince me the credit can be framed around the Z2 invariant and its first observation, I would move it up.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first on the grounds that Z2 topology of band structures reshaped electronic-structure thinking and materials searches, and he places the moire graphene entry third.
responses.response: I agree that the Z2 classification reshaped how electronic structure is thought about, and that the effect has been seen in many material families by transport and ARPES. Where I differ is on what remains open. For B051 I share his own caveat: the nature of the correlated and superconducting states is still debated, and a field this young risks a prize that later needs qualification. For B008 the interpretation is stable but the credit allocation is not. By comparison the clock result has no live dispute about what was measured, only about how its benefits will be used, which is the safer ground for a prize.

responses.point: Lindroth places the optical lattice clock first, crediting Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's precision record, and notes that independent laboratories confirm the performance.
responses.response: I agree on the core case and want to add a qualification on attribution. Lindroth's list points to Lemonde, Takamoto and Lisdat; that is a fair reminder that the 10^-18 level was a community achievement, but it does not alter who conceived the concept (Katori) and who made it the accuracy and many-body benchmark (Ye). I would resist widening the credit just because the field is crowded; the citation should name the invention and the realization, as mine does, without claiming the whole of optical timekeeping.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as an instrument-and-construction landmark that opened neutrino astronomy, with Halzen as the intellectual driver and Karle and Spiering credited for detector and collaboration roles, though he cannot independently verify the exact division of credit.
responses.response: I respect the detector achievement and share his instinct that large instrument advances deserve recognition. But I would not rank it above the clock. Source identification is still developing, with TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 not yet a settled population picture, and the division of credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, which Pearce himself says he cannot verify, is the kind of uncertainty that makes me cautious. It remains a serious candidate for a later year; I leave it off my alternatives only because the two I list have clearer cases now.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clear, original and widely reproduced architecture that underlies most superconducting quantum processors, with a clean Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf trio.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is original, mature and widely reproduced and that the three names map onto theory, first strong coupling and the later toolbox. My reservations are about timing relative to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which makes the neighbourhood less open than the clock result, and about colleagues such as Devoret and Huard being associated with the field. I list it as my second alternative rather than my preference. Johansson and I are both at Chalmers, so I flag below that I should not be the neutral judge of his field.

uncertainties: Whether the Hall and Hansch recognition of 2005 makes the lattice clock look like an extension rather than a distinct invention.
Whether Wineland, Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto and Yb-clock groups should be credited and whether the committee can express that within two names.
Whether the redefinition of the second is close enough that the committee would prefer to wait for the metrology decision.
Whether B008 can be framed in a way that handles the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal, since it would otherwise be my leading alternative.
I rely on background knowledge for the exact accuracy records and the sequence of independent confirmations, not on a verified record.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connections to flag from my profile: I am at Chalmers, as is committee member Goran Johansson, whose field of superconducting circuits is the subject of B004 (circuit QED), which I list as an alternative, so I would consider recusing myself from that part of any deliberation. My own field is transmission electron microscopy and I was identified as president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy in 2024, so I have a possible bias toward B019 (aberration-corrected electron optics), which I ranked first at opening; I do not propose it here. No specific personal or institutional connection to the clock candidates or to the topological-insulator candidates is apparent from the provided profile.
